    AI Overview
    A pied-à-terre (French for "foot on the ground") is a small second home, apartment, or condominium, typically located in a major city, that is used for part-time, temporary, or seasonal residence rather than as a primary, year-round home. While often associated with the wealthy, these units serve as convenient, low-maintenance urban bases for commuters, frequent travelers, or those who enjoy a city lifestyle without living there full-time. 
    Key Characteristics and Usage 
    • Definition: It is a secondary residence that is not the owner's primary address.
    • Purpose: Used for work-week stays, short-term visits, or to avoid long commutes.
    • Location: Often found in high-end urban neighborhoods.
    • Real Estate Context: In cities like New York, condos are generally more flexible with pied-à-terre usage, while co-ops may restrict or prohibit them. 
    Pied-à-terre in NYC Real Estate (Current Developments)
    As of April 2026, New York State officials are negotiating a "pied-à-terre tax" as part of the state budget to help close a projected $5.4 billion budget deficit. 
    • Tax Proposal: Governor Hochul and city officials are proposing a yearly surcharge on residential properties worth $5 million or more that are not used as a primary residence.
    • Target: The tax primarily targets non-residents, international buyers, or wealthy individuals who use luxury condos as occasional homes.
    • Impact: The tax is intended to generate roughly $500 million annually. 
    Origins
    The term originated in the 18th century, referring to soldiers who would dismount their horses ("mettre pied à terre") to occupy temporary lodging.
